summary: Defines a Telnet option that lets one side ask the other to echo back what it receives. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The Telnet ECHO option lets the two ends agree whether one end should send received characters back to the other. It is off by default, and both directions are managed independently.

why does telnet need suppress go ahead with echo
how does telnet remote echo work
subtitle: Lets Telnet peers negotiate which end echoes characters received over the connection.

tldr.problem: In an interactive Telnet session, the remote process may need to control how typed characters are echoed to the user's terminal.
tldr.mechanism: The ECHO option lets either end request or refuse remote echoing, separately for each direction of the connection.
tldr.outcome: Echoing is off by default, and both ends must avoid enabling remote echoing in both directions because that can create an endless echo loop.

today: RFC 857 is listed as an Internet Standard in the unit metadata. The metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Remote Echo Is Needed
sections.content:
A Network Virtual Terminal is described as having a keyboard and printer that may echo characters locally. In interactive situations, the remote process may need to control how characters appear on the user's terminal.

The ECHO option lets the parties agree that characters typed at one end will be echoed by the system at the other end.
sections.plainLanguage: Some interactive programs need to decide how typed characters appear at the user's terminal. The ECHO option lets the remote system take part in that decision.

sections.title: Requesting or Refusing Echo
sections.content:
The option code is 1. WILL ECHO says the sender will echo data it receives, while DO ECHO asks the other end to do so. WON'T ECHO and DON'T ECHO refuse or stop echoing.

The default is no echoing over the Telnet connection. Either side can ask for a change; if the other side refuses, the connection remains in non-echo mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The commands let one side ask the other to echo received characters or stop echoing them. If the other side refuses, no remote echoing starts.

sections.title: Echo Directions and Loop Prevention
sections.content:
A Telnet connection carries data in both directions, and each direction can be in echo mode independently. The option controls whether one end echoes for the other; it does not control whether an end echoes locally for itself.

If both ends echo characters received from the other, each echoed character can return indefinitely. Implementations should prevent the two ends from entering that combination.
sections.plainLanguage: Each direction has its own echo setting, and local echo remains a local decision. If both ends echo for each other, characters can bounce back and forth without stopping.

sections.title: Character-at-a-Time Interaction
sections.content:
Remote echoing is not usually enough by itself to create character-at-a-time interaction. The RFC says the SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD option will normally also be needed.

The RFC recommends coordinating changes with the option commands so that data is not briefly echoed twice or handled in the wrong mode.
sections.plainLanguage: To echo each typed character remotely as it is entered, the connection will usually need both ECHO and SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD. Coordinated changes help avoid confusing duplicate echoes.
